anchor: O that those lips had language
title: Occasion and date
short: Written early in 1790 when Cowper's cousin Ann Bodham sent him a portrait of his mother, who had died over fifty years before; published 1798.
body: Ann Bodham, née Donne, of Mattishall in Norfolk, was Cowper's cousin on his mother's side. In February 1790 she sent him a miniature of his mother, and on 27 February he wrote thanking her, saying he had kissed the picture and hung it where it would be the last thing he saw at night and the first in the morning. He wrote the poem soon after. It was published in 1798 and reprinted with other poems in 1799. The opening apostrophe, wishing the painted lips could speak, establishes the poem's theme: art preserves the face but not the voice.

title: Art against time
short: Cowper blesses painting for defeating time's power to 'quench' his mother's look, a traditional topos of art's immortality.
body: The idea that art preserves what time destroys is ancient (Horace's 'exegi monumentum', Odes III.30) and was central to Shakespeare's Sonnets. Cowper applies it to portrait painting: the 'meek intelligence' of the eyes survives Time's 'tyrannic claim'. The parenthesis shapes the syntax so that the poem's first long sentence ends in the present: 'here shines on me still the same'. The theme is taken up in the last lines, where Time 'has but half succeeded in his theft'.

title: remembrancer
short: A thing or person that reminds; the picture is addressed as a guest who brings memory back.
body: The OED records 'remembrancer' in the sense of one who reminds, or a memento; it was also the title of officials of the Exchequer charged with recording debts, which faintly colours the idea of a debt to be paid. The portrait is addressed as a 'welcome guest' who 'bidst' (commands) the poet to write. The command is accepted 'not willingly alone, / But gladly', as if it came from the mother herself.

title: artless song
short: An unaffected, simple poem; the claim to artlessness is a convention of sincere elegy.
body: 'Artless' means free from artifice, natural and sincere; it was a term of praise in the age of sensibility. Cowper's modesty is conventional but also characteristic of the poem's plain conversational couplets, quite unlike the elevated diction of most eighteenth-century elegy. The word stands in pointed contrast to the 'art' of the painter just praised (l. 8): painting can immortalise, and the poem only offers a 'frail memorial' (l. 72).

title: Elysian
short: From Elysium, the classical paradise of the blessed dead; the reverie will be as happy as Elysium, and will bring him to her.
body: In Homer (Odyssey IV.563) and Virgil (Aeneid VI) Elysium is the abode of the virtuous dead. Cowper, an Evangelical Christian, uses the classical word as a figure for a dreamlike bliss in which the dead seem present. 'Steep me' suggests immersion, as in a drug or a bath. The reverie is admitted to be 'momentary', and 'Fancy', not faith, produces it, so the poem is honest about its consolation.

title: The mother's death
short: Ann Cowper, née Donne, died on 13 November 1737, after the birth of her son John; William was not yet six.
body: Cowper was born on 26 November 1731 at the rectory of Great Berkhamsted, Hertfordshire, where his father John Cowper was rector. His mother died at about 34-36 (sources differ) a few days after giving birth. The section recalls the child's experience: being told she was dead, hearing the bell tolled for her burial and seeing the hearse from the nursery window. The questions to her spirit ('wast thou conscious ...?') and the reply from the painted smile, 'Yes', are the emotional centre of the poem's first half.

title: Wretch even then
short: Cowper sees his whole life as wretched from the start, a hint of the religious despair that oppressed him from 1773.
body: Cowper suffered severe depressive breakdowns in 1763 and 1773, and after a dream in 1773 he believed himself irrevocably damned. The phrase 'Wretch even then, life's journey just begun' projects that sense of lifelong misery back to infancy. It prepares for the poem's later contrast of the mother who has reached harbour and the son 'tempest-toss'd'. Biographers have linked the early loss of his mother to his later melancholy, though this is an interpretation, not Cowper's own claim.

sources.cite: James King, William Cowper: A Biography (Durham, NC: Duke UP, 1986)

title: The funeral bell
short: Memory of the funeral: the passing bell, the hearse, and the child turning from the nursery window.
body: The details are concrete and plainly told, which is the source of their power. The 'long, long sigh' and 'a last adieu' are then questioned in the next line: 'But was it such?--It was.' The broken exchange, question and answer, shows the poet correcting the child's hope that she would return with the adult's knowledge. The repeated 'adieu ... Adieus and farewells' turn on the idea of heaven as a place where partings are unknown.

title: The servants' promise
short: The maidservants, grieving at the child's distress, told him his mother would soon return; he believed them day after day.
body: Eighteenth-century households often concealed death from small children. 'What ardently I wish'd, I long believed' is a moral generalisation in the Johnsonian manner, about the will's power over belief. 'Dupe of to-morrow even from a child' compresses this into an epigram: the child is deceived by hope as the adult is (compare Johnson's Vanity of Human Wishes and Rasselas, which also treat the credulity of hope).

sources.cite: John D. Baird and Charles Ryskamp, eds., The Poems of William Cowper, vol. III: 1785-1799 (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1995), commentary on the poem

title: infant sorrows
short: His childhood grief, imagined as a stock or supply that is used up until he learns submission.
body: 'Stock' is a commercial figure: grief is a store spent day by day. 'Infant' here means childish, of early childhood. 'Submission to my lot' is a Christian virtue, but the next line keeps the emotional truth: 'though I less deplored thee, ne'er forgot'. ('Deplored' meant lamented, wept for.) The couplet ends the paragraph of childhood grief with the theme of memory that governs the rest of the poem.

title: the pastoral house
short: The rectory at Berkhamsted, the house of a pastor; the family lost it when Cowper's father died in 1756.
body: 'Pastoral' plays on two senses: belonging to a pastor (the parsonage), and idyllic, as in pastoral poetry. On John Cowper's death in 1756 the living passed to another clergyman and the family left; 'Children not thine have trod my nursery floor'. 'Short-lived possession!' sets the parsonage, held only by right of office, against the permanent 'record' kept by memory, an idea extended in 'memory's page' (l. 68).

title: Robin; bauble coach
short: The family gardener who pulled the little boy to school in a small toy-like carriage, dressed in a scarlet cloak and velvet cap.
body: 'Bauble' means a toy or showy trifle, so the 'bauble coach' is a child's small carriage, drawn by hand. Cowper went as a small child to a local school in Berkhamsted; after his mother's death he was sent away to a boarding school at Markyate, an unhappy experience he later recalled. The detail of clothing ('scarlet mantle warm, and velvet capp'd') shows the mother's care for the child's comfort and appearance, preparing for the catalogue of her kindnesses that follows.

title: confectionary plum
short: A sugar-plum, a small sweet of boiled sugar; the adjective means made by a confectioner.
body: 'Confectionary' (more often 'confectionery' in modern spelling) is here an adjective, 'of the nature of a confection'. With 'the biscuit' it forms part of the mother's 'morning bounties', tiny gifts. The 'fragrant waters' of the next line are scented waters (such as rose or lavender water) used to wash the child's face. Critics have praised this catalogue of domestic particulars as one of the most moving uses of ordinary detail in eighteenth-century verse.

title: cataracts and breaks
short: Her love flowed constantly, like a smooth stream, never broken by the waterfalls and rapids that changes of mood produce.
body: 'Humour' means temper or mood, a sense derived from the old physiology of the four humours. The image of love as a river is sustained: 'flow', 'fall', 'roughen'd', 'cataracts' (waterfalls, rapids) and 'breaks' (broken water). The tribute is to an unvarying temper; it may also glance, by contrast, at Cowper's own fluctuating moods. 'Legible in memory's page' (l. 68) then shifts the metaphor from river to book.

title: numbers
short: Numbers are verses, metrical lines, from the Latin use of numeri for rhythm and metre.
body: The use of 'numbers' for verse was standard in eighteenth-century poetic diction (Pope's 'I lisp'd in numbers'). 'Such honours ... as my numbers may' (supply 'pay') is a modest tribute: the poet's verse can only do what it can. The phrase links back to the 'artless song' of l. 13 and forward to the 'frail memorial' of l. 72, a sequence of modest self-descriptions running through the poem.

title: a frail memorial
short: An echo of Gray's Elegy, where 'Some frail memorial' marks the graves of the humble dead.
body: Gray's Elegy Written in a Country Churchyard (1751), l. 78, speaks of 'Some frail memorial still erected nigh' to protect the bones of the poor. Cowper's adoption of the phrase sets his poem among elegies for the obscure: his mother, 'little noticed here', is honoured in heaven. The contrast of heaven and earth ('Not scorn'd in heaven') is a Christian turn on the Elegy's theme of unrecognised worth.

title: tissued
short: Tissued means woven with a pattern, often of gold or silver thread; the dress was embroidered or brocaded with flowers.
body: The OED gives 'tissue' in its early sense of a rich cloth interwoven with gold or silver, and 'tissued' as woven or decorated in this way. The child pricked out the outlines of the dress's flowers ('The violet, the pink, and jessamine') onto paper with a pin, a pastime of tracing patterns by pinpricks. Jessamine is jasmine. The scene is the last and most intimate of the remembered moments, with the mother's smile and touch.

anchor: Thy unbound spirit into bonds again
title: The refusal to wish her back
short: Cowper asks whether he would bring back those days, admits he might, and decides it would be unkind to recall her soul to earthly bondage.
body: The passage dramatises an inner debate in broken syntax and dashes ('I would not trust my heart--the dear delight / Seems so to be desired, perhaps I might.--'). The resolution is Christian: life on earth is 'So little to be loved', and the soul freed from the body would be constrained 'into bonds again'. The idea of the body as the soul's prison is Platonic and Pauline (Romans 7:24; 2 Corinthians 5:1-8). It is the poem's ethical turn, from desire for the past to acceptance of loss.

Bible, King James Version, 2 Corinthians 5:1-8

title: The voyage simile
short: An extended epic simile: the mother is a ship that has crossed the ocean of life and lies at rest in a paradisal harbour.
body: A 'bark' is a ship; 'Albion' is the ancient poetic name for Britain. The simile of life as a voyage and death as reaching harbour is a commonplace of Christian and classical writing. The ship rests 'quiescent' in a 'well-haven'd isle / Where spices breathe', an exotic picture recalling the Spice Islands of the East Indies, with 'airs impregnated with incense' suggesting the incense of worship as well as fragrant winds. The simile sets up the contrast with the poet's own wrecked voyage that follows.

title: A quoted line from Garth
short: The quotation marks show borrowing: Garth's Dispensary (1699) has the line 'Where billows never break, nor tempests roar'.
body: Samuel Garth's mock-heroic poem The Dispensary (1699) has, in canto III, the line 'Where billows never break, nor tempests roar'. Cowper reverses the order of the two clauses ('Where tempests never beat nor billows roar') but marks it as a quotation. The borrowing gives his image of heaven as a harbour a familiar literary authority; the line was much quoted in the eighteenth century and Bartlett's Familiar Quotations records it.

title: thy loved consort
short: Cowper's father, the Rev. John Cowper, who died in 1756 and is pictured as a ship anchored beside hers.
body: John Cowper, rector of Great Berkhamsted from 1722 and a chaplain to George II, remarried in 1741 and died in 1756. 'Long since has anchor'd by thy side' completes the ship image and reunites the parents in heaven. The thought becomes the son's consolation in l. 106: 'But oh, the thought, that thou art safe, and he!' That the father is placed beside the mother, though he had married again, reflects the conventional Christian hope of the reunion of the faithful in heaven rather than biographical detail; the father plays a small part in the poem as a whole.

title: The poet's shipwreck
short: The poet's life is a storm-driven ship without a compass, a figure for the religious despair in which Cowper believed himself excluded from salvation.
body: 'Devious' means straying from the path (Latin de via). 'Sails ripp'd, seams opening wide, and compass lost' is a precise picture of shipwreck; the 'current's thwarting force' drives him further from 'a prosperous course'. After 1773 Cowper believed himself irrevocably rejected by God, which gives the image its theological sense: he is 'scarce hoping to attain that rest'. The same imagery returns, still more desolately, in 'The Castaway' (1799), his last original poem, about a sailor washed overboard.

title: Noble and heavenly descent
short: His pride is not in royal ancestry but in being 'the son of parents pass'd into the skies'.
body: Cowper's maternal family, the Donnes of Norfolk, claimed descent from Henry III and other medieval nobility, a lineage biographers record and Cowper knew. 'Deduce my birth' means trace my descent. He disclaims that worldly pride in favour of a higher one: descent from parents now in heaven. The couplet adapts an old moral commonplace (true nobility is virtue, not blood) to the Evangelical language of salvation.

title: Fancy's half-victory
short: The conclusion: by memory and fancy he has relived his childhood, and Time, the thief, has taken his mother but not her power to comfort him.
body: 'Time unrevoked has run / His wonted course' answers the earlier wish ('Could Time, his flight reversed, restore the hours'). 'Without the sin of violating thine' means without wronging her heavenly rest by recalling her. The 'mimic show' is the portrait. The final antithesis, 'Thyself removed, thy power to soothe me left', resolves the poem's opening complaint that the lips lack language: the picture cannot speak, but it consoles. Critics have connected the poem's reliving of childhood with the Romantic poetry of memory that followed it.
